365.title: Mostly quiet
365.hook: speak rarely and only what's needed, and not about people (Enchiridion 33)
365.howItsDone: Some people who practice Stoicism treat silence as their default in conversation and make a habit of not discussing absent people, especially not blaming, praising or comparing them.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was diviner, and the one question you never need to ask. Your line was reason has already answered.

Three hundred sixty-five. A whole calendar's worth of days, worth one breath of its own. Now a small test. Think back over yesterday's conversations, the kitchen, the office, the group chat. How many were about someone who wasn't there? It's not a trick question, and the answer can be a little uncomfortable. The handbook's thirty-third section is a long set of small rules for how a person of character talks, laughs and listens. The next few days take it a piece at a time. It starts with the mouth.
screen: `THREE HUNDRED SIXTY-FIVE.` → `HOW MUCH TALK WAS ABOUT SOMEONE ELSE?` → `MOSTLY QUIET.`

segments.voice: Section thirty-three begins: decide now on a certain character and pattern for yourself, and keep to it, whether you're alone or with other people. Everything after is a sketch of that character. The first stroke: let silence be the general rule, Epictetus says, or say only what's needed, in few words. That's not a vow of silence. It's a default, like a resting position. When you do talk, rarely and when the moment calls for it, skip the ordinary topics: gladiators, horse races, athletes, food and drink. Those were the everyday topics of his world, he implies. Translate them into today and you'll recognize the list. He isn't banning sports. He's noticing how many hours of a life go into conversation that leaves nobody changed. Above all, not about people. Don't blame them, don't praise them, don't compare them. That's the one he leans on hardest. Then a gentler line: if you can, turn your friends' conversation toward something worthwhile, and among strangers, keep quiet. Why would a Stoic care so much? Talk about absent people is almost always talk about things outside your control: what they did, what they're like, what they deserve. It feeds judgment and envy, and it rarely helps the person being discussed. Mostly quiet isn't cold. It leaves room for the conversations that matter.
screen: `CHOOSE A CHARACTER, AND KEEP IT.` · `SILENCE AS THE DEFAULT.` · `SKIP THE GLADIATORS AND HORSE RACES.` · `ABOVE ALL, NOT ABOUT PEOPLE.` · then, large: `MOSTLY QUIET.`

segments.voice: Let the noise of the day thin out, and picture the moment later when a conversation turns toward someone who isn't there, with its little pull, the thrill of the story. See yourself letting it pass, saying nothing, or asking the other person how they're doing instead. Then rest in the quiet you're sitting in now.
Mostly quiet. Epictetus' first rule for a person of character: silence by default, few words when needed, and not about people. Today's word.
Your line: let silence be the rule. Fewer words leave more room to listen. See you tomorrow.

366.title: Yes means yes
366.hook: don't laugh much or loudly, and avoid swearing oaths when you can (Enchiridion 33)
366.carry: a word that doesn't need help
366.howItsDone: Some people on a Stoic path avoid oaths and emphatic promises and try to keep their plain word instead; Quakers and some other Christian communities affirm rather than swear.

segments.voice: Yesterday's lesson was mostly quiet: silence by default, few words, and not about people. Your line was let silence be the rule.

I swear I'll be there. I swear on my mother. Hand on heart, I promise. You stack these up when you want to be believed, and the funny thing is, the more you pile on, the less sure everyone gets. Someone who says I swear three times in one sentence can end up being the one people double-check. Section thirty-three keeps sketching a person of character, and today it gets to two small habits: how you laugh, and how you promise.
screen: `I SWEAR. I SWEAR ON MY MOTHER.` → `THE MORE YOU PILE ON, THE LESS SURE.` → `YES MEANS YES.`

segments.voice: First, laughter. Don't laugh much, Epictetus says, or at many things, or without restraint. That can sound grim, so look closely. He isn't banning joy. The worry seems to be laughing that runs away with a person: laughing to fit in, laughing at someone, laughing so loudly you're no longer really there. A smile you mean is still in your power. A roar to impress the room may not be. Then oaths. Refuse to swear an oath, he says, altogether if you can, and if you can't, as far as you can. He doesn't stop to explain. One way to read it: if your plain word is good, an oath adds nothing. If it isn't, an oath won't fix it. Piling on swears is a quiet admission that a simple yes isn't enough. So the Stoic aims to be someone whose yes is the whole promise. A neighbor said something close. In the Sermon on the Mount, in the King James Bible, Jesus says: "But let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay." Christians have taken that in different ways. Quakers, and some Mennonite and Amish communities, decline to swear oaths and affirm instead. Other Christians take oaths in court and office and read the verse as being about honesty. The United States Constitution makes room for both: a president may swear, or affirm. Two traditions, each in its own house, arriving at the same plain picture: a word that doesn't need help.

segments.voice: Think of one recent promise, I'll call you back, I'll finish it by Friday, I'll be there, and picture the person you made it to. Without adding a single I swear, just decide to keep it: no drama, no extra words, just a yes that holds. If there's a promise you can't keep, picture yourself telling them so, simply.
Oath. What Epictetus says to refuse as far as you can, letting your plain word carry the promise instead. Today's word.
Your line: a word that doesn't need help. A plain yes can carry the whole promise. Day three hundred sixty-six.

367.title: Ask, don't tell
367.hook: don't dwell on your own deeds and dangers; others don't enjoy them as you do (Enchiridion 33)
367.carry: hands the stage to someone else
367.howItsDone: People practicing Stoicism sometimes set themselves a simple conversational habit: fewer stories about their own exploits and more questions about the other person.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was oath, and the plain word that doesn't need one. Your line was a word that doesn't need help.

Everyone has been on the receiving end of this. Dinner, a long table, and someone is telling the story of their near miss on the highway. Or the marathon. Or the time they told the boss exactly what they thought. It's the third time you've heard it, and it's getting longer. The uncomfortable part: everyone has also been the one telling it. Section thirty-three, still sketching how to behave in company, has a line for exactly this.
screen: `DINNER, AND THE NEAR-MISS STORY.` → `THE THIRD TIME YOU'VE HEARD IT.` → `ASK, DON'T TELL.`

segments.voice: In company, Epictetus says, don't keep bringing up your own deeds and your own dangers, often and at length. The reason is disarmingly honest: however pleasant it is for you to recall your dangers, it isn't as pleasant for other people to hear about them. No grand theory. Just an observation anyone can check at the next dinner party. Your own stories glow for you because you were in them. For everyone else, they're secondhand. Right after comes another line. Avoid playing for laughs, he says. It slides easily into vulgarity, and it tends to lower the respect the people around you have for you. The common thread is the spotlight. Telling your adventures and working the room for a laugh both turn a conversation into a stage with one performer. Now the turn. The handbook doesn't say ask in so many words; that's how this path carries it. But it fits the man Epictetus admired most. Socrates, in Plato's dialogues, is famous for asking questions, so many that it became a method named after him. If you're not telling, you have room to ask. How was your week? What happened next? What was that like for you? A question hands the stage to someone else. It's a small trade: one story fewer told, one more heard all the way to the end.
screen: `DON'T DWELL ON YOUR OWN EXPLOITS.` · `YOUR DANGERS THRILL YOU, NOT THEM.` · `DON'T PLAY FOR LAUGHS.` · `SOCRATES ASKED.` · then, large: `ASK, DON'T TELL.`

segments.voice: Think of someone you'll talk with today, a coworker, a friend, a parent, a child, the person at the counter, and picture the moment you'd usually start telling them your news. Picture asking them a question instead, and actually waiting for the answer. Keep one ready: how are you, really, or what's been the best part of your week?
Ask. Enchiridion thirty-three: don't keep telling your own deeds and dangers. Others don't enjoy them as much as you do. Leave room to ask. Today's word.
Your line: hands the stage to someone else. That's what a good question does. That's day three hundred sixty-seven.

368.title: He missed the rest
368.hook: if told someone speaks ill of you, say: he didn't know my other faults (Enchiridion 33)
368.howItsDone: People practicing Stoicism sometimes answer reported criticism with self-deprecating humor, as Epictetus suggests, rather than defending themselves point by point.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was ask: your own stories please you more than your listeners. Your line was hands the stage to someone else.
screen: `ASK — HANDS THE STAGE TO SOMEONE ELSE.`

segments.voice: A screenshot arrives with a short note above it: thought you should know. Someone has been saying things about you. It's easy to start drafting the reply right there in your head, point by point, with receipts and a closing line. Section thirty-three of the handbook has a one-line answer for this moment, far older than any screenshot. It's short, a little ridiculous, and a very good comeback.
screen: `THOUGHT YOU SHOULD KNOW.` → `ALREADY DRAFTING THE REPLY.` → `HE MISSED THE REST.`

segments.voice: If someone tells you that a certain person is speaking badly of you, Epictetus says, don't defend yourself against what was said. Instead, answer: he obviously didn't know my other faults, or he wouldn't have mentioned only these. Why it works: a defense keeps the argument alive. You go point by point, they answer, the circle grows. His reply steps out of the contest entirely. It agrees, cheerfully, that you have faults, more than the critic knows, so there's nothing left to fight about. The joke is on yourself, and nobody else gets hurt by it. The verb he uses for defend yourself belongs with apologia, a speech of defense, the word in the title of Plato's Apology, where Socrates defends himself at his trial. Epictetus' advice, roughly: skip the apologia. What it isn't: self-hatred, or ignoring a fair point. If the critic is right about something, you've learned something. If they're wrong, nothing that belongs to you has been touched. That idea came up a couple of weeks ago, with the insult: it's not the words that harm you, but your judgment that you've been harmed. Today's line is that idea with a grin on its face. It costs nothing, and it ends the conversation better than any receipt.
screen: `DON'T DEFEND YOURSELF.` · `HE DIDN'T KNOW MY OTHER FAULTS.` · `SKIP THE APOLOGIA.` · `A FAIR POINT TEACHES; A WRONG ONE CAN'T HARM.` · then, large: `HE MISSED THE REST.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one criticism that still stings, and notice where it lands in your body, and the urge to argue with it. Then try Epictetus' answer inside, he missed the rest, and see if the sting changes; you might even smile. If part of it was fair, let that part stay, and let the rest go.
Apologia. The Greek word for a speech of defense, which Epictetus says to skip: they didn't know my other faults, or they'd have mentioned those too. Today's word.
Your line: better than any receipt. A fair point teaches; a wrong one can't touch what's yours. Day three hundred sixty-eight, done.

369.title: Wait before pleasure
369.hook: when a pleasure beckons, pause, and picture both the enjoying and the regret after (Enchiridion 34)
369.howItsDone: Some people practicing Stoicism put a short delay between an urge and acting on it, and in that pause picture both the enjoyment and how they'll feel afterward.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was apologia, the defense Epictetus says to skip: he missed the rest. Your line was better than any receipt.

The kitchen is dark except for the open fridge, and the last slice of cake is right there. Or it's the tab with the shopping cart, or the one more episode button counting down from ten. There's a moment, maybe half a second long, between the urge showing up and your hand moving. It's easy to miss entirely. Section thirty-four of the Enchiridion lives inside that half second, and asks you to stretch it out.
screen: `THE OPEN FRIDGE, THE LAST SLICE.` → `HALF A SECOND BEFORE THE HAND MOVES.` → `WAIT BEFORE PLEASURE.`

segments.voice: When the impression of some pleasure arrives, Epictetus says, be careful not to be swept off by it. Let the thing wait for you. Give yourself a little delay. He doesn't say refuse. He says wait. In the delay, call to mind two times. The time when you'll be enjoying the pleasure. And the time after, when you've had it, and you're sorry, and you're scolding yourself. Both are real. Look at both. Then set a third picture against them: how glad you'll be, and how well you'll think of yourself, if you hold off. Three scenes, and you get to watch all of them before you choose. And the honest ending. If, after all that, it seems the right time to enjoy the thing, Epictetus allows it. Just take care, he says, that its sweetness and its pull don't overpower you, and remember how much better it is to know you've won that small contest. This isn't a rule against pleasure. It's a rule against being carried. The pleasure that survives the wait is one you've chosen.
screen: `LET THE PLEASURE WAIT FOR YOU.` · `PICTURE THE ENJOYING, AND THE REGRET.` · `PICTURE THE GLADNESS OF HOLDING OFF.` · `IF YOU TAKE IT, DON'T BE CARRIED.` · then, large: `WAIT.`

segments.voice: Think of an urge you know well, a snack, a scroll, a purchase, a drink, a reply typed too fast, and picture it arriving. Run the three pictures slowly: the enjoying, the after and how you might feel, and the gladness of having waited. You don't need to decide anything now; just practice watching all three before your hand moves.
Two pictures, Epictetus says to call to mind before giving in: the moment of the pleasure, and the moment after, sorry and self-scolding. Today's word.
Your line: wait. Half a second can grow into a real choice. See you tomorrow.

370.title: No need to hide
370.hook: if you've judged it right, don't hide doing it (Enchiridion 35)
370.howItsDone: People practicing Stoicism sometimes check whether they are hiding a right action out of fear of disapproval, and if so, do it openly; if the wish to hide signals that the act is wrong, they don't do it.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was two pictures: the enjoying, and the regret after. Your line was wait.

A teenager in a school cafeteria sees the new kid eating alone. She'd like to go sit with him. She'd also like nobody to see her do it. A man leaves the office at five sharp to coach his daughter's soccer team, and slips out the side door so the others won't notice. People do the right thing, and then do it a little in hiding, as if they've been caught. Section thirty-five of the Enchiridion is only a few lines long, and it's aimed at exactly that side door.
screen: `THE NEW KID EATING ALONE.` → `OUT THE SIDE DOOR AT FIVE.` → `NO NEED TO HIDE.`

segments.voice: When you've judged that something ought to be done, and you're doing it, Epictetus says, never avoid being seen doing it, even if the many are going to think badly of it. The logic is tidy. Either the thing is wrong, or it's right. If it's wrong, don't do it at all. If it's right, the people who'll find fault with it are mistaken, so why be afraid of them? Hiding a right action quietly hands a vote to people whose opinion, by your own judgment, is wrong. It echoes earlier sections. Section thirteen asked you to be content to seem foolish about outside things, and section twenty-two warned that anyone who takes up this way of life will be laughed at. Today is the practical follow-through. You've already accepted that people may think you odd. So stop ducking. There's a test hidden in the sentence, too. If you notice the urge to hide something you're doing, ask why. Sometimes it's only fear of what people will say, and his answer is: then do it in the open. But sometimes the wish to hide is the first quiet sign that the thing isn't right, and his answer to that is just as plain: then don't do it. This isn't about showing off; the handbook gets to that soon. It's about not shrinking. A right thing done openly also gives the next person permission to do it too.
screen: `JUDGED RIGHT? DON'T AVOID BEING SEEN.` · `WRONG: DON'T. RIGHT: WHY FEAR CRITICS?` · `YOU'VE ALREADY ACCEPTED SEEMING ODD.` · `THE URGE TO HIDE IS A TEST.` · then, large: `NO NEED TO HIDE.`

371.carry: for the sake of the fellowship
371.howItsDone: Some people practicing Stoicism take the smaller share at shared meals and let others choose first, as a small way of honoring the company and the host.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was the many, whose disapproval needn't make you hide a right act. Your line was without the side door.

A platter comes around the table. Four pieces of chicken left, and one of them is clearly the biggest. Everyone sees it. Everyone pretends not to. There's a small, silent negotiation going on, and you may have been on both sides of it. Epictetus, of all people, uses this moment to teach a bit of logic. Section thirty-six of the Enchiridion starts like a textbook on reasoning and ends at a dinner party.
screen: `FOUR PIECES LEFT. ONE IS BIGGEST.` → `A LOGIC LESSON AT DINNER.` → `THE TABLE MATTERS.`

segments.voice: Take two statements: it is day, it is night. Joined with or, it is day or it is night, they make a perfectly good statement. Joined with and, it is day and it is night, they make a false one. Same pieces, different combination. The value depends on how they're joined. In the same way, Epictetus says, at a shared meal, taking the biggest portion may have value for your body taken alone. But joined to the table, to the company and the host, it loses that value. So the larger share is to be avoided, for the sake of the fellowship of the meal. When you eat with someone, he says, don't only weigh what the food on your plate is worth to your body. Keep in view the respect owed to your host. The meal isn't just food. It's a relationship being kept, one plate at a time. Back in section fifteen, life was a banquet, and the lesson was to take a modest share when the dish reaches you. Today goes one step further: the smaller portion isn't only self-control, it's a way of honoring the people at the table. And a look back at the week, since today closes it: mostly quiet. Yes means yes. Ask, don't tell. He missed the rest. Wait. No need to hide. Every one of them, like today's, is about living well alongside other people.
screen: `DAY OR NIGHT: TRUE. DAY AND NIGHT: FALSE.` · `THE BIGGEST PORTION, JOINED TO THE TABLE.` · `KEEP THE HOST IN VIEW.` · `THE SMALLER PORTION HONORS THE TABLE.` · then, large: `THE TABLE MATTERS.`

segments.voice: Picture the next meal you'll share, at home, at work, anywhere: the table, the faces, the food going around. See yourself quietly taking the smaller portion, or letting someone else choose first, with no announcement. Notice how it feels to put the table ahead of your plate for a moment, then let the picture go and just breathe.
Banquet. Life as a shared meal, Epictetus says elsewhere; the biggest portion may suit your body, but not the fellowship of the table. Today's word.
Your line: for the sake of the fellowship. The host and the company count too. Day three hundred seventy-one, and the week is done.
